cards.title: 2.1 Statistics, population and sample
body: **Statistics** is collecting, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical data. In the opening story, one son *collects* the weekly profits, the second *organises* them in a table, the third *interprets* them ("profit above 250 Nakfa in 5 of 20 weeks, a 25% chance").
**Population:** every member of the group being studied. **Sample:** the part we actually collect data from, chosen to represent the population.
**Census:** data from every member (accurate but slow and costly). **Sampling:** data from some members (fast and cheap, but it must be representative).
**Simple random sampling (lottery method):** number every member, draw numbers from a hat (or random numbers) so that every group of the chosen size has the same chance.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: To choose a sample of 50 students from a list of 1000, a researcher picks a random starting point and then every 20th name. This is:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Sampling interval k = population ÷ sample size = 1000 ÷ 50 = 20.

**Step 2:** Choosing every k-th member after a random start is systematic sampling.

**Step 3:** Answer: systematic sampling.

**Tip:** Stratified = divide into groups and sample each group; cluster = choose whole groups at random.

cards.title: Sampling methods
body: A **census** studies the whole population; a **sample** studies part of it (cheaper and faster). A sample must be **representative**, otherwise the results are **biased**.

**Simple random sampling:** every member has the same chance (lottery method or random numbers). **Systematic sampling:** choose every k-th member from a list after a random start. **Stratified sampling:** divide the population into groups (strata, e.g. grades) and sample from each group in proportion to its size. **Cluster sampling:** randomly choose whole groups (e.g. some schools) and study everyone in them.
**Example:** a school has 300 Grade 9 and 200 Grade 10 students; a stratified sample of 50 takes 30 from Grade 9 and 20 from Grade 10.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Types of data
body: A **variable** is a characteristic that changes from member to member (height, blood type, number of children). One value is a **datum**; the collection is the **data**.
**Qualitative (categorical):** a label or category — sex, blood type, Zoba, disease status.

**Quantitative (numerical):** a count or measurement. It is **discrete** if the values can be counted (number of children, pages, calls: 0, 1, 2, …) and **continuous** if it can take any value in a range (height, time, rainfall, income measured exactly).
**Quick test:** "how many?" → discrete; "how much / how long / how heavy?" → continuous.

cards.title: 2.2.2–2.2.3 Frequency tables
body: **Frequency** = how many times a value occurs. **Relative frequency** = frequency ÷ total; **percentage** = relative frequency × 100%. **Cumulative frequency** = running total up to that value.
**Activity 2.8 (blood types of 40 students):** O 16, B 10, A 9, AB 5 — percentages 40%, 25%, 22.5%, 12.5%. Most common O, least common AB.

**Example 2.6 (corrected):** dog 11, cow 10, goat 4, sheep 3, cat 2 (30 children). The **least** liked animal is the **cat** (the book says "cow"), the number who like dogs **or** cats is $11 + 2 = 13$ (the book adds cows and dogs: 21), and the proportion who like sheep is $\frac{3}{30} = 0.1$.
**Example 2.7:** women with fewer than 3 children: $7 + 8 + 11 = 26$ women (52%); more than 1 child: $11 + 14 + 8 + 2 = 35$ (70%).

cards.title: Grouped data: limits, boundaries, class mark

steps.text: Class **limits** are the end numbers written in the table: 20 – 29.
Class **boundaries** close the gaps between classes: halfway between 29 and 30 is 29.5, so the class runs from 19.5 to 29.5. **Class width** = upper boundary − lower boundary = 10.
**Class mark** (midpoint) $= \frac{20 + 29}{2} = 24.5$ — the value that stands for the whole class in calculations and graphs.

cards.title: Reading a grouped table (Example 2.8)
body: With classes 0–10, 10–20, … the width is 10. Marks of at most 40: add the frequencies up to the class 30–40: $2 + 10 + 21 + 19 = 52$ (the book's line says "less than or 60" but means 40). Wages of 850 or more in Example 2.9: $1 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 10$ workers.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following represents a quantitative continuous variable?

options.A: The yearly amount of rainfall in Asmara
options.B: The number of children in a family
options.C: The number of bicycles parked in a school compound
options.D: The blood type of a student

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand quantitative continuous variables**
A continuous variable is a quantitative variable that can take any value within an interval, representing a measured quantity (not countable).

**Step 2: Evaluate the options**
'Number of children' and 'Number of bicycles' are countable integers, making them discrete.
'Blood type' is categorical, making it qualitative.
'Yearly amount of rainfall' is measured (e.g., $$540.5\text{ mm}$$) and can take any real value in an interval.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the quantitative continuous variable is **The yearly amount of rainfall in Asmara**.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Classes are 10–19, 20–29, 30–39. What is the class width?
cards.why: Class width = difference between consecutive lower class limits: 20 − 10 = 10 (or between the class boundaries 9.5 and 19.5).

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Frequencies are 3, 7, 5, 5. What is the cumulative frequency of the third class?
cards.why: Cumulative frequency adds all frequencies up to that class: 3 + 7 + 5 = 15.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: What is the midpoint (class mark) of the class 20–29?
cards.why: Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2 = (20 + 29)/2 = 24.5. Class marks are used as x when finding the mean of grouped data.

cards.title: Frequency distributions
body: Raw data are organised in a **frequency distribution table**: each value or class with its **frequency** (how many times it occurs). **Relative frequency** = frequency ÷ total; **cumulative frequency** = running total.

For **grouped data** choose 5–15 classes of equal width: width ≈ (largest − smallest) ÷ number of classes, rounded up. Each class has lower and upper **limits** (e.g. 20–29), **boundaries** (19.5–29.5) and a **class mark** (midpoint 24.5).
Variables are **qualitative** (categories) or **quantitative**: **discrete** (counted, e.g. number of children) or **continuous** (measured, e.g. height).

cards.title: Worked example: build a frequency table
Quick check
cards.q: A researcher studies the health status of students in a school and classifies the data as 'Healthy', 'Mildly Ill', or 'Severely Ill'. What type of variable is this?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the nature of the data**
The values 'Healthy', 'Mildly Ill', and 'Severely Ill' describe non-numerical attributes or characteristics of the students.

**Step 2: Compare with statistical definitions**
Variables that allow for classification based on attributes are qualitative (or categorical) variables. Quantitative variables must represent numerical counts or measurements.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Since this data classifies individuals into categories, the variable is **Qualitative (Categorical)**.

cards.title: 2.3 Statistical graphs
body: A **pie chart** is a circle divided into sectors; each sector angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, so the area is proportional to the frequency.
A **bar graph** labels the categories on the horizontal axis and the frequency (or relative frequency) on the vertical axis; bars have equal width and gaps between them.
A **histogram** is used for grouped (continuous) data: the bars stand on the class boundaries and touch each other. A **frequency polygon** joins the midpoints of the tops of the histogram bars.
An **ogive** (cumulative frequency curve) plots cumulative frequency against upper class boundaries; it is used to estimate the median and quartiles.
**Example:** 60 students: 15 walk, 30 take the bus, 15 cycle. Angles: walk 15/60 × 360° = 90°, bus 180°, cycle 90°.

cards.title: Pie chart: angle = percent × 3.6°
body: Each sector angle $= \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}} \times 360°$: Food $35\% \to 126°$, Rent $90°$, Savings $72°$, Misc. $54°$, Education $18°$. With an income of 1500 Nakfa: food $0.35 \times 1500 = 525$, education 75, rent and savings $375 + 300 = 675$ Nakfa (the book's line prints "75" for the rent part).

steps.text: **Histogram:** bars stand on the class boundaries and **touch** (no gaps), heights = frequencies.
**Frequency polygon:** join the midpoints of the bar tops (class marks 5, 15, 25, …) with straight lines, and close it down to the axis at both ends.
The tallest bar is the **modal class** (20 – 30, frequency 21).

cards.q: A family's monthly income is $$1500\text{ Nakfa}$$. They spend $$35\%$$ of their income on food. How much money do they spend on food monthly?
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the parameters**
Total Income = $$1500\text{ Nakfa}$$
Percentage spent on food = $$35\% = 0.35$$

**Step 2: Calculate the food expenditure**
$$\text{Food Expenditure} = \text{Total Income} \times \text{Percentage}$$
$$\text{Food Expenditure} = 1500 \times 0.35$$
$$\text{Food Expenditure} = 525$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
The family spends **$$525\text{ Nakfa}$$** on food.

cards.title: Choosing and reading a graph
body: **Which graph?** Categories (favourite subject, type of fuel) → bar graph or pie chart (pie chart when you want to show parts of a whole). Grouped numerical data (heights, marks) → histogram or frequency polygon. Change over time (monthly rainfall) → line graph. Running totals, median and quartiles → ogive.

**Drawing a histogram:** mark the class boundaries on the horizontal axis (e.g. 9.5, 19.5, 29.5, …) and frequency on the vertical axis; draw touching bars whose heights are the frequencies. The tallest bar shows the **modal class**.
**Reading an ogive:** for n = 40 values, the median is read at cumulative frequency 20, the lower quartile at 10 and the upper quartile at 30; interquartile range = Q₃ − Q₁.
**Misleading graphs:** a vertical axis that does not start at 0, or bars of unequal width, can make small differences look large — always read the scale.

cards.title: 2.4.1 Mean, median and mode
body: A **measure of central tendency** is one value that represents the whole data set.
**Mean:** $\bar{x} = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_N}{N} = \frac{\sum x_i}{N}$. Example 2.15: $\frac{30}{10} = 3$ children.

**Median:** sort the data. If $N$ is **odd**, it is the middle value, in position $\frac{N + 1}{2}$. If $N$ is **even**, it is the mean of the values in positions $\frac{N}{2}$ and $\frac{N}{2} + 1$. (The book's first definition swaps "odd" and "even"; its step-by-step rule is right.)
**Mode:** the most frequent value. There may be two modes (Example 2.21: 1 and 3) or none (Example 2.22).

cards.title: Worked example: the median of 40 values (Example 2.19)
cards.problem: Battery lives of 40 phones, sorted: 1.6, 1.8, 2.2, …, 4.7. Find the median.

steps.text: $N = 40$ is even: the middle positions are 20 and 21.
Counting in the sorted list: $x_{(20)} = 3.4$ and $x_{(21)} = 3.4$.

cards.title: One extreme value (Activity 2.22, Exercise 2.5 Q3)
body: Class A ages 16, 18, 17, 18, 19, **38**: mean 21, median 18. Class B with 20 instead of 38: mean 18, median 18. One extreme value pulls the mean but not the median. Likewise 1–10 has mean 5.5, but changing 10 to 100 makes the mean 14.5 while the median stays 5.5.

cards.title: 2.4.2 Range, variance and standard deviation
body: Two data sets can have the same centre and very different **spread** (dispersion).
**Range** $R$ = largest − smallest.
**Variance** = average squared distance from the mean: $$\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{N}$$
**Standard deviation** $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$, in the same units as the data (variance is in squared units, e.g. hour²).
**Shift and scale:** adding a constant to every value changes the mean but **not** the variance; multiplying every value by $k$ multiplies the standard deviation by $|k|$ (Exercise 2.6 Q3, Q4).

(The book divides by $N$ and calls this the population variance; Example 2.27 calls it "sample" standard deviation and refers to Example 2.25 — it means Example 2.26. A sample variance divides by $n - 1$ instead.)

cards.title: Two banks, same average wait
body: Both banks have mean 7.15 min, median 7.2 and mode 7.7, but the range at Bank A is $7.7 - 6.5 = 1.2$ min and at Bank B $10.0 - 4.2 = 5.8$ min (the book labels both lines "Bank A"). Bank B's waiting times vary much more.

cards.title: Reading the table
body: Deviations always add to 0 (a check on the mean). $\sigma^2 = \frac{394}{8} = 49.25$ hour², $\sigma = \sqrt{49.25} \approx 7.02$ hours.

cards.title: Averages
body: Raw data mean $\bar x=\dfrac{\sum x}{n}$. Grouped: $\bar x=\dfrac{\sum f x}{\sum f}$ (use class midpoints as $x$).
Median: middle value when ordered (or $L+\dfrac{\frac{n}{2}-F}{f}\times c$ for grouped). Mode: most frequent class.

cards.title: Trick — which average?
body: Mean uses every number (sensitive to outliers). Median is the “typical middle”. Mode is the fashion — useful for sizes/shoes. If the question says “average” with no adjective, they usually want the mean.

cards.title: Spread
body: Range $= \max-\min$. Variance uses squared deviations; standard deviation $\sigma$ is the square root (same units as the data). Larger $\sigma$ → more spread.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Find the arithmetic mean of the following children counts of 10 families: $$3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 3, 4, 2, 3, 3$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the mean formula**
$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{N}$$

**Step 2: Sum the values**
$$\sum x_i = 3 + 4 + 2 + 5 + 1 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 30$$

**Step 3: Divide by the count $$N = 10$$**
$$\bar{x} = \frac{30}{10} = 3$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The arithmetic mean of children count is **$$3$$**.

**Step 1: Check sorting and count**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Calculate the population variance of the following set of numbers: $$6, 7, 8, 9, 10$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Calculate the mean of the dataset**
$$\bar{x} = \frac{6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 10}{5} = \frac{40}{5} = 8$$

**Step 2: Calculate the squared deviations from the mean**
$$(6 - 8)^2 = (-2)^2 = 4$$
$$(7 - 8)^2 = (-1)^2 = 1$$
$$(8 - 8)^2 = (0)^2 = 0$$
$$(9 - 8)^2 = (1)^2 = 1$$
$$(10 - 8)^2 = (2)^2 = 4$$

**Step 3: Sum the squared deviations**
$$\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10$$

**Step 4: Divide by the count $$N = 5$$ to find variance ($$\sigma^2$$)**
$$\sigma^2 = \frac{10}{5} = 2$$

**Step 5: Final Result**
The variance of the dataset is **$$2$$**.

cards.title: 2.5.1 Experiments, sample spaces and events
body: An **experiment** is a process with well-defined outcomes (toss a coin, roll a die). The **sample space** $S$ is the set of all outcomes; an **event** is a subset of $S$.
Coin: $S = \{H, T\}$. Die: $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. Two coins: $\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$. A **simple event** has one outcome; the **null event** $\varnothing$ has none (Example 2.30: an even factor of 9).
**Operations:** $A \cap B$ (both), $A \cup B$ (either or both), $A'$ (not $A$). $A$ and $B$ are **mutually exclusive** if $A \cap B = \varnothing$.

cards.title: Listing outcomes with a tree
body: Each student passes (P) or fails (F): 2 branches, then 2, then 2, so $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ outcomes: PPP, PPF, PFP, PFF, FPP, FPF, FFP, FFF. The same tree lists D/N items (Example 2.29) or the sexes of three children.

cards.title: 2.5.3–2.5.4 Experimental and theoretical probability
body: **Experimental probability** = relative frequency $= \frac{\text{times the outcome happened}}{\text{number of trials}}$. Example 2.31: 35 of 100 students chose blue: $0.35$.
**Theoretical probability** (equally likely outcomes): $$P(E) = \frac{n(E)}{n(S)} = \frac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}$$
Always $0 \le P(E) \le 1$: 0 = impossible (a black card from green, yellow and blue cards), 1 = certain.
**Comparing (Activity 2.34):** 13 sevens in 50 rolls of two dice gives $0.26$; theory gives $\frac{6}{36} \approx 0.17$. With more trials the experimental value gets closer to the theoretical one.

cards.title: Two dice: count the cells
body: 36 equally likely outcomes. Sum 7 appears 6 times ($P = \frac{1}{6}$), sum 11 twice, so $P(7 \text{ or } 11) = \frac{8}{36} = \frac{2}{9}$. A total of 8 appears 5 times ($\frac{5}{36}$).

steps.text: $P(B)$ counts every outcome in $B$ — the overlap is now counted twice.
Subtract it once: $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B).$$ If $A$, $B$ are mutually exclusive the overlap is empty and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

cards.title: Only for independent events
body: The rule $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$ holds when one event does not change the chances of the other: two different dice, a coin and a die, or drawing **with replacement**. The book states it for "events A and B" in general; it is not true for, e.g., "even" and "greater than 3" on one die ($\frac{2}{6} \ne \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}$).

cards.title: 2.5.6 Counting: the multiplication principle
body: If one choice can be made in $m$ ways and then another in $n$ ways, together there are $m \times n$ ways; for more steps keep multiplying. Breakfast: $4 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$ choices; outfits: $2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12$.
Arranging $n$ different objects in a line: $n!$ ways (FAST: $4! = 24$ words).

cards.title: Worked example: Example 2.44(b) (corrected)
cards.problem: The letters of STATISTICS are arranged at random. Probability that the arrangement begins with SSS?

steps.text: After SSS the other 7 letters are T, T, T, I, I, A, C: $\frac{7!}{3!\,2!} = \frac{5040}{12} = 420$ arrangements (the book gets 84).
Check another way: the first three letters are S with probability $\frac{3}{10} \cdot \frac{2}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{120}$.

cards.title: Probability
body: $$P(A)=\frac{n(A)}{n(S)}\qquad 0\le P(A)\le 1$$
Complement: $P(A')=1-P(A)$. If $A$ and $B$ cannot happen together (mutually exclusive), $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$. If independent, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

body: “At least one” → use the complement: $1-P(\text{none})$. Write the sample space if $n$ is small (dice, coins).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If you roll a fair die followed by tossing a coin, what is the probability of rolling a '4' on the first die and getting a 'Head' on the coin?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the nature of events**
Rolling a die and tossing a coin are independent events because the outcome of one does not affect the outcome of the other.

**Step 2: Calculate individual probabilities**
Probability of rolling a 4 on a fair 6-sided die: $$P(4) = \frac{1}{6}$$
Probability of getting a Head on a fair coin: $$P(\text{Head}) = \frac{1}{2}$$

**Step 3: Apply the multiplication rule for independent events**
$$P(4 \cap \text{Head}) = P(4) \times P(\text{Head})$$
$$P(4 \cap \text{Head}) = \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{12}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The probability of both occurring is **$$\frac{1}{12}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In how many distinguishable ways can the letters of the word 'STATISTICS' be arranged in a line?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Count the total number of letters ($$n$$)**
The word 'STATISTICS' has $$n = 10$$ letters.

**Step 2: Identify the repeated letters and their frequencies**
Letter 'S' appears $$3$$ times.
Letter 'T' appears $$3$$ times.
Letter 'I' appears $$2$$ times.
Letter 'A' appears $$1$$ time.
Letter 'C' appears $$1$$ time.

**Step 3: Apply the distinguishable permutations formula**
$$\text{Arrangements} = \frac{n!}{n_1! \times n_2! \times n_3! \times \dots}$$
$$\text{Arrangements} = \frac{10!}{3! \times 3! \times 2!}$$
$$\text{Arrangements} = \frac{3628800}{6 \times 6 \times 2} = \frac{3628800}{72} = 50400$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The number of distinguishable arrangements is **$$50400$$**.

glossary.meaning: Statistics is the collection, presentation , analysis and interpretation of the numerical data.
Population is the collection of all elements (individuals, objects, areas, etc.) under consideration in a study.
Variable is the characteristic of interest of an element that can assume different values for the different elements in the population or sample.
Frequency distribution table is a summary table that shows the number of observations that belong in the different classes (groups).
If an event is a set containing only one element of the sample space, then it is called a simple event.
The part of the population that data are collected from.
The value halfway between neighbouring class limits.
The square root of the variance; spread in the data's units.
The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
A selection where order does not matter.
